story.title: Malaga
story.lede: Nana Losa turns 80 this year, and the whole ʻāiga is going home to Savaiʻi for it. She has asked you for one thing: greet the family in Samoan. On the way you’ll visit every branch of the family, from the Bay to Savaiʻi, and learn a little at each house.

stops.title: Sunday at Aunty Mele’s
intro: Sunday afternoon in East Palo Alto. Aunty Mele’s family is home from church and the toʻonaʻi, the Sunday meal, is on the table.
The aunties are sitting on the couch by the door.

words.en: excuse me (passing in front of people)
words.note: Say it with your head and shoulders a little lower.

choose.why: That’s goodbye. You just got here!
Aunty laughs. “Hey is for your friends. For your elders: Tālofa lava.”

talk.prompt: Answer her, and ask her back.

choose.why: That says “I’m Mele.” She’s Mele!
Leai is “no.” She asked how you are.

talk.narr: To reach the table you have to pass in front of the aunties on the couch.

choose.act: Lower your head and shoulders a little and say “Tulou.”
Walk past quickly without a word.
choose.why: The aunties notice. Tulou is the word for passing in front of them.
That’s “come inside,” what Aunty said to you.

talk.sm: ʻUa ʻou fiafia ʻauā ʻua ʻe sau.

choose.why: You asked that already. Now: thank you very much.

stops.culture: Tulou is what you say as you pass in front of people who are sitting, often with your head and shoulders a little lower. With this many aunties on the couch, you’ll say it a lot at Aunty Mele’s.

keep.en: a frangipani from Aunty’s pot by the door

stops.title: Siva practice in Carson
intro: Carson, next to Long Beach in Los Angeles County, is home to one of the biggest Samoan communities on the mainland.
Aunty Lupe is teaching the cousins a siva, a dance, for Nana’s birthday. Practice is in the church hall.

words.en: the last dance of a celebration
words.note: Danced by someone honored, often the person the party is for.

talk.sm: Tālofa lava! ʻO ai lou igoa?

choose.why: That’s her question, back to her.
That’s a price, not an age! Twenty is luasefulu.

talk.narr: She starts the count, and the cousins’ hands move slowly through the air: tasi, lua, tolu...

choose.why: Lima is five, and it’s also the word for hand. But after tolu comes fā.
Fitu is seven. After tolu (three) comes fā (four).

talk.narr: Aunty explains: at Nana’s party the last dance is the taualuga, and Nana will dance it. The family dances around her.

talk.prompt: When Nana dances the taualuga, who is the star?

choose.act: Nana. Everyone else dances around her, lower and smaller, so she shines.
You: get in front so everyone sees your new moves.
choose.why: Aunty laughs. Tonight the taualuga is Nana’s.

stops.culture: At Nana’s party the taualuga, the last dance, is hers. The family dances around her, keeping lower and clowning a little, so she shines.

keep.en: the taualuga song, saved on your phone

stops.title: Nana’s photo album
intro: Nana Losa lives in the Salt Lake Valley, with the Wasatch Mountains behind her house. Polynesian families have lived in Utah since the 1800s, and today it has one of the biggest Samoan communities on the mainland.
Before the trip, Nana wants you to know who’s who.

words.en: brother of a man, sister of a woman

choose.why: That’s what the host says. This is Nana’s house.
Foʻi means “too,” and Nana hasn’t said how she is. Say: ʻOloʻo manuia faʻafetai.

talk.narr: Nana opens the photo album.

talk.sm: ʻO loʻu tuagane lenei, ʻo Ioane.
ʻO loʻu uso lenei, ʻo Malia.

talk.prompt: Uncle Ioane talks about Nana. What does he call her?

choose.why: Tuagane is a woman’s brother. A man’s sister is his tuafafine.
Uso is a brother or sister of the same sex. Nana and Ioane are sister and brother.

talk.sm: Mālō! E nofo Ioane i Savaiʻi.
talk.en: Well done! Ioane lives in Savaiʻi.

talk.sm: Alu e asiasi i lou ʻāiga.

choose.why: Nana raises an eyebrow. She was hoping for ʻIoe.

stops.culture: Samoan has its own words for brothers and sisters: uso for a sibling of the same sex, tuafafine for a man’s sister, tuagane for a woman’s brother. The bond between a brother and a sister is called the feagaiga.

keep.en: Nana’s fine mat, to carry home to Savaiʻi

stops.title: Choir practice in the rain
intro: It’s raining in Federal Way, south of Seattle, with Mount Rainier hidden in the clouds. The Seattle–Tacoma area has one of the biggest Samoan communities in the country.
Uncle Tavita leads his church’s choir, and practice is tonight.

choose.sm: ʻOu te fiafia i le timu.
ʻOu te lē fiafia i le timu.

choose.why: That’s “it’s all gone,” for the market. The rain is not gone.
True, it is Wednesday. But he asked if you sing.

talk.narr: He hands you a hymn book. Then he pats his wrist: he left his watch at home.
Your phone says 7:00.

choose.why: Tasi is one. Seven is fitu.
That’s his question, back to him.

talk.narr: Everyone stands, and the choir starts the hymn in four parts.

choose.why: Not yet! Thank him first.

stops.culture: Mālō praises something someone has done: Mālō le pese! for a song, Mālō le faʻauli! for the drive home. Uncle Tavita praised you, and you thanked him back.

stops.title: The festival in Peninsula Park
intro: Summer in Portland. Every year the Portland-Vancouver Samoan Festival fills Peninsula Park in North Portland with music, dancing and food stalls.
Aunty Fetū has a stall of buns and coconuts. You need something to bring the family.

choose.sm: Tālofa lava. E iai ni tou pani, faʻamolemole?
choose.en: Hello. Do you have any buns, please?

choose.why: Aunty waits. Start with tālofa, and end with faʻamolemole.
That’s “what’s your name?” Ask the price first.

talk.sm: E lua tālā i le pani e tasi.

talk.prompt: Buy a bun and a coconut.

choose.sm: ʻAumai se pani ma se niu, faʻamolemole.
choose.en: A bun and a coconut, please.

choose.why: Aunty laughs. Two dollars is a fair price, and it all goes to her church.

talk.sm: ʻO le niu, e lua foʻi tālā.
talk.en: The coconut is two dollars too.

choose.why: Two for the bun and two for the coconut: fā, four.
Valu is eight. Two and two is fā.
Her buns aren’t gone yet! Say: thank you too.

stops.culture: An oso is a food gift you bring when you visit family. Aunty Fetū’s buns are the start of yours.

stops.title: A call home from New York
intro: Your cousin Sina is at college in New York, a long way from the rest of the ʻāiga. It’s late and she’s homesick.
You call Nana together.

choose.why: Mālō is “well done.” She’s sad, not proud. Tālofa e means “oh, poor you.”

talk.narr: You call Nana. Her face fills the screen.

choose.sm: Tālofa lava, Nana. ʻO ā mai ʻoe?

choose.why: Nana is in Utah. She can’t come in!

talk.sm: Manuia faʻafetai. Sina, ʻo ā mai ʻoe?
talk.en: Fine, thanks. Sina, how are you?

talk.sm: ʻOu te alofa iā te ʻoulua.

choose.sm: ʻOu te alofa foʻi iā te ʻoe, Nana.

choose.why: That thanks someone for eating. Tell her you love her too.
Late! But that’s not goodbye.

stops.culture: Faʻalavelave are the big family events: weddings, funerals, a title bestowed, a birthday like Nana’s. Sina is already saving for the flight to Savaiʻi.

keep.en: a picture of you and Sina on the call

stops.title: Coconut and fire in Lāʻie
intro: Lāʻie, on Oʻahu’s north shore. Uncle Pita works in the Samoan village at the Polynesian Cultural Center, where he shows visitors how to climb a coconut tree and make fire with two sticks.
More Samoans live in Honolulu than in any other US city.

talk.narr: The fale has no walls: only posts and a high round roof. Fala, woven mats, cover the floor.

choose.why: Uncle tucks his own feet under and smiles. You follow his lead and sit cross-legged.

choose.act: Stay standing and talk to him.
choose.why: Uncle pats the mat next to him. If you ever do have to talk standing up, “Tautala tū atu” means excuse me for speaking standing.

talk.sm: ʻO le niu lenei. ʻE te fia inu?
talk.en: This is a coconut. Would you like a drink?

choose.why: He offered you a drink, not the time.

talk.narr: He husks it on a sharp stake in a few seconds, opens it, and hands it to you.
Then he rubs a stick along a groove in a dry log until it smokes, and blows the dust into a flame.

stops.culture: Uncle Pita sits cross-legged on the fala and shows you where to sit. Samoan fale, Hawaiian hale and Māori whare are the same old word for house.

stops.title: Evening prayer under Rainmaker Mountain
intro: Pago Pago Harbor on Tutuila, American Samoa, under Rainmaker Mountain. American Samoa is a US territory: the money is the US dollar, and Samoan is spoken in every village.
You’re helping at a relative’s fale up the coast when the village’s high chief, the matai, arrives.

words.en: sacred; the quiet time for evening prayer
words.note: Sā is also the past tense marker.

talk.narr: The matai steps up into the fale.

choose.why: Sau is the everyday word for come. For a chief, the respect word is Afio mai.
Maliu mai is for an orator, a tulāfale. For a high chief: Afio mai.
Suafa is the respect word for a name. Use it for his name, not your own.

talk.sm: Mālō. ʻO fea ʻe te sau ai?
talk.en: Good. Where do you come from?

talk.narr: He laughs. Then a bell rings across the village: it’s the sā, the time for evening prayer. Families go inside, and the road goes quiet.

choose.act: Sit quietly with the family until the bell rings again.
Walk down the road to the store.
choose.why: In this village, sā means everyone stays put and quiet until the second bell.

talk.prompt: Thank him, as you would an elder.

choose.en: Thank you very much. Good health to you.

choose.why: Fā is a quick bye between friends. Mālō le soifua is warmer.

stops.culture: Respect words (gagana faʻaaloalo) are used for others, not for yourself: a chief’s name is his suafa, his house his maota, and for come you say afio. With children, people use the everyday words.

stops.title: Hello in five languages
intro: Suva, Fiji. The University of the South Pacific belongs to twelve Pacific countries, Sāmoa among them, and students come here from all of them.
Your cousin Iosefa studies here. He’s brought his friend Mere, who’s Fijian.

words.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te sau ai?

talk.sm: Tālofa lava! ʻO laʻu uō lenei, ʻo Mere.
talk.en: Hello! This is my friend, Mere.

choose.why: You’ve only just met!

talk.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te sau ai?

talk.prompt: She’s learning Samoan too. Answer her.

choose.why: Mere laughs. “I’m the one from Fiji!”

talk.narr: Iosefa counts on his fingers: bula in Fiji, mālō e lelei in Tonga, kia ora in Aotearoa, aloha in Hawaiʻi, and tālofa at home.

choose.why: That’s Māori. You’ll hear it at the next stop.
That’s Fijian, Mere’s hello.

talk.prompt: You’re flying to New Zealand next.

choose.sm: ʻOu te alu i Niu Sila.

choose.why: That’s where you’re from. He asked where you’re going.

stops.culture: Samoan, Tongan, Māori and Hawaiian are Polynesian languages, close cousins. Fijian is a more distant cousin: house is fale in Samoan, whare in Māori, hale in Hawaiian and vale in Fijian.

keep.en: a cowrie shell from Suva Harbour

stops.title: After church in South Auckland
intro: Auckland, Aotearoa. Samoans are the biggest Pacific community in New Zealand, and South Auckland is one of its hearts. Every March, high schools from across the city perform at Polyfest.
It’s Sunday. After the service, the minister and his wife greet everyone at the door.

words.en: you (to a minister, teacher or guest)
a minister’s or chief’s wife (respect word)

choose.why: Uō is “friend.” A minister is lau susuga.

talk.sm: Susū mai. ʻO ā mai ʻoe?

choose.sm: Manuia faʻafetai. ʻAe ā lau susuga?

choose.why: Close! To a minister, put lau susuga in place of ʻoe.

talk.en: Come and have something to eat.

talk.narr: At the table, the minister is asked to say grace.

choose.act: Wait, head bowed, until grace is over.
Start on the chop suey: you’re hungry.
choose.why: Everyone at this table waits for the lotu, the grace, and the amene at the end.

talk.narr: After the meal, the faletua comes by your seat.

talk.prompt: Tell her the food was good.

choose.why: That’s for the market!

stops.culture: A minister is called the feagaiga, the covenant, and his wife the faletua. Lau susuga is “you” said with respect.

keep.en: a piece of siapo (tapa cloth) from the faletua

stops.title: Taro at the Apia market
intro: Apia, the capital of Sāmoa. Maketi Fou, the main market, is piled with taro, bananas and coconuts.
Nana asked you to bring taro to Savaiʻi. Malia has the best at her stall.

choose.sm: Tālofa lava. E iai ni tou talo, faʻamolemole?
choose.en: Hello. Do you have any taro, please?

choose.sm: E iai ni tou pani, faʻamolemole?
choose.en: Do you have any buns, please?
choose.why: That’s the Portland festival! Here you want talo.
That asks what day it is.

talk.sm: E sefulu tālā i le ʻato e tasi.

talk.prompt: A whole basket for ten tālā is a good price.

choose.en: That’s cheap! I’ll take it, please.

choose.why: Taugatā means expensive. Ten tālā for a basket of taro is a good price.
Save “thank you too” for when she thanks you.

stops.culture: Sāmoa’s money is the tālā, and a tālā is 100 sene. Malia’s prices are chalked on a board by the taro.

keep.en: a basket of taro for Savaiʻi

stops.title: The ʻava welcome
intro: Your traveling party, the malaga, reaches the village where Nana’s cousins live. They welcome the malaga with an ʻava ceremony.
An orator, a tulāfale, speaks for the village, his fue (fly whisk) over one shoulder.

words.note: With the same spelling, ʻava also means beard.

words.en: May it go well! (said before drinking ʻava)

talk.narr: The orator stands and welcomes the malaga in a long, beautiful speech.

talk.prompt: What do you do during the speech?

choose.act: Whisper to your cousin about the food.
choose.why: Your cousin shakes her head: not during the speech.

talk.narr: An older orator arrives late from the next village.

choose.why: Afio mai is for a high chief, an aliʻi. An orator gets Maliu mai.
Sau is the everyday word. For an orator: Maliu mai.

talk.narr: The ʻava is mixed in the tānoa and served in a coconut-shell cup, called out to each person in turn. Yours comes.

talk.prompt: What do you do with the cup?

choose.act: Pour a few drops onto the mat, say “ʻIa manuia,” and drink.
Gulp it down without a word.
choose.why: Your uncle shows you: a few drops first, ʻIa manuia, then drink.

stops.culture: Orators (tulāfale) speak for this village. Chiefs (aliʻi) and orators each have their own respect words: afio for a chief, maliu for an orator.

stops.title: The umu on Sunday morning
intro: Savaiʻi, the big island. Nana’s brother Ioane is the matai of the family here.
Before church, the young men light the umu, an oven of hot stones on the ground, for the toʻonaʻi.

words.en: taro leaves baked in coconut cream

talk.prompt: Greet him the way you would an elder.

choose.why: He’s the matai. Tālofa lava, and a wish for his health.

talk.narr: After church the toʻonaʻi is laid out on the mats: palusami, taro and fish from the umu. Papa Ioane sits at the head. The young people serve.

choose.act: Papa Ioane, then the other elders and guests.
You do: you helped with the umu.
choose.why: At Papa Ioane’s, the elders and guests eat first and the young ones serve.
ʻAi is the everyday word. Taumafa is the respect word for eat.

talk.narr: Everyone waits while Papa Ioane says grace.
Later, full of palusami.

talk.prompt: Tell him the food was good.

stops.culture: At Papa Ioane’s, Sunday is church, the toʻonaʻi and rest: the umu is lit early, the elders eat first, and the afternoon is quiet.

keep.en: a taro leaf from the palusami

stops.title: Nana’s 80th
intro: Everyone is here: Aunty Mele from California, Uncle Tavita from Washington, Sina from New York, the cousins from Auckland and Suva, Papa Ioane and the whole village.
Nana stands, and asks you to welcome the family, in Samoan.

talk.narr: Chiefs, orators, the minister and the whole ʻāiga are seated on the mats. You stand. You start with the highest.

talk.prompt: The first words of your welcome:

choose.why: Start with the highest: chiefs first.
Warmer and higher for a gathering like this. Chiefs first.
You’ve welcomed the chiefs. Now the orators.
Not for a gathering of elders! Susū mai welcomes everyone with respect.

talk.narr: A murmur of approval. Afio mai, maliu mai, susū mai.

choose.sm: ʻO le aso fānau lenei o Nana.

choose.why: True, but that’s not why everyone came.

talk.prompt: And thank them for coming all this way.

choose.why: Not the food, not yet!

talk.narr: Nana takes the ʻie tōga from Utah and spreads it out for everyone to see.

talk.sm: Mālō! ʻOu te alofa iā te ʻoe.
E suamalie feiloaʻiga ae ʻoʻona tēteʻaga.
talk.en: Meeting is sweet, but parting is bitter.

stops.culture: Nana’s welcome starts with the chiefs, then the orators, then everyone: Afio mai, maliu mai, susū mai. You’ve now spoken with an aunty, a matai, an orator, a minister and Nana, each with their own words.
